lead: A light wave in a fiber carries two speeds at once. The crests of its sine wave travel at the phase velocity. The pulse that carries the bits travels at the group velocity. Timing in a link — how long a bit takes to reach the receiver — follows the group velocity, not the phase velocity. This chapter defines both speeds, ties them to the fiber's effective index, and shows how to compute pulse delay over a length of fiber.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for the propagation constant β, and Chapter 1.6 for the effective index of a mode.

sections.h3: Crests and envelopes move at different speeds

blocks.text: A sine wave of one frequency has a definite propagation constant β, measured in rad/m. Its crests move forward at the phase velocity.

blocks.where: vp is phase velocity in m/s; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; β is the propagation constant in rad/m; c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s is the speed of light in vacuum; n_eff is the dimensionless effective index of the mode.

blocks.text: A single frequency carries no information. A pulse, meaning a short burst of light, is a band of frequencies around a carrier. The whole band travels as one envelope, at the group velocity. Only a few universities teach this in detail.

blocks.where: vg is group velocity in m/s; dω/dβ is the derivative of angular frequency with respect to propagation constant, taken at the carrier frequency.

blocks.text: Rewriting the derivative against wavelength gives the working form used in link design.

blocks.where: N_g is the dimensionless group index; λ is the vacuum wavelength in metres; dn_eff/dλ is the slope of effective index against wavelength, in 1/m. For silica, that slope is negative, so N_g is slightly larger than n_eff.

blocks.text: A pulse launched at time zero reaches the far end after a group delay.

blocks.where: T is the group delay in seconds; L is the fiber length in metres; N_g is the group index; c is 3.00 × 10^8 m/s. This T, not L/vp, is the number a rise-time budget uses.

sections.h3: Reading the numbers in a link

blocks.text: In a typical fiber n_eff = 1.46 and N_g = 1.48 differ by about 1 percent, so vp and vg sit close together. Over 10 km that 1 percent is roughly 0.5 µs of extra delay — small once, but repeated in every span of a long route.

items: Use vg for anything that carries bits: bit slots, rise-time budget, synchronisation.
Use vp only for the phase of one continuous wave, as in interference and grating formulas.
Both n_eff and N_g shift when the waveguide geometry changes; that is waveguide dispersion, handled in Unit 2, Signal Degradation in Optical Fibers.

figure.caption: The crests of the sine wave move at the phase velocity; the pulse envelope that carries the bits moves at the group velocity, which sets the arrival time at the receiver.

spec.aria: A sinusoid block leads to phase velocity vp = ω/β, and a pulse envelope block leads to group velocity vg = dω/dβ.
spec.title: Phase and group velocity

examples.question: At λ = 1550 nm a fiber has effective index n_eff = 1.46 and group index N_g = 1.48. Take c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s. Find (a) the phase velocity, (b) the group velocity, (c) the pulse delay over L = 10 km.
steps: Length in metres: L = 10 km = 10,000 m.
examples.answer: vp = 2.05 × 10^8 m/s, vg = 2.03 × 10^8 m/s, and the pulse delay over 10 km is 49.3 µs.
examples.check:
c = 3.00e8
neff = 1.46
Ng = 1.48
L = 1.0e4
vp = c / neff
vg = c / Ng
t = L / vg
print(round(vp/1e8, 2) * 1e8)
print(round(vg/1e8, 2) * 1e8)
print(round(t*1e6, 1) * 1e-6)

traps: Using n_eff instead of N_g in L N_g/c understates the delay; the group index governs pulses.
Phase velocity is not the speed of information — a monochromatic wave has no bits on it.
In silica N_g is slightly above n_eff; a smaller N_g points to a sign slip in dn_eff/dλ.
Put L in metres and λ in metres before dividing; 10 km is 10,000 m, not 10.

quiz.q: Define phase velocity in terms of ω and β.
quiz.a: vp = ω/β; it is the speed at which a point of constant phase moves.

quiz.q: Write the group index in terms of n_eff and λ.
Why does a pulse travel at the group velocity and not the phase velocity?
quiz.a: A pulse is a band of frequencies; the band's envelope moves at dω/dβ, while the crests inside it move at ω/β.

quiz.q: A fiber has N_g = 1.47. Find the group delay over 2 km using c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s.
Two fibers share n_eff = 1.45 but have N_g = 1.46 and N_g = 1.49. Which adds more pulse delay over the same length, and why?
quiz.a: The N_g = 1.49 fiber, because T = L N_g/c rises in direct proportion to N_g.

quiz.q: Why are vp and vg nearly equal in a silica fiber?
quiz.a: Because dn_eff/dλ is small, so N_g differs from n_eff by only about 1 percent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Group velocity is what dispersion measurements actually record: a phase-shift method reads the delay at several wavelengths and differentiates it. Soliton links balance group-velocity dispersion against self-phase modulation (see Unit 6). Search next for the group index of silica, the Sellmeier equation, and the modulation phase-shift dispersion measurement.
